_meta.why: The plaque is person-keyed and several people report their year on it is wrong. Years are the stable spine; people are attached to years and can be moved.

role_values.president: Led the student government that year
role_values.regent: Held the student seat on the WKU Board of Regents - a separately elected office from 1968 until the two merged
role_values.unresolved: Shares a year with another name and the split is not yet established

_meta.student_regent_history: The student regent seat was created by state legislation reported in committee in February 1968 and filled in April 1968 by William Menser. It carried no vote for at least four years - students were campaigning for voting power in February 1970 and the Herald was still reporting 'Student Regent May Get Vote' in February 1972. Because it was separately elected, several plaque years carry two names: one president and one regent.

leaders.name: Jim Haynes
leaders.note: First president of the Associated Students of Western Kentucky University, elected 18 May 1966, seven weeks after President Kelly Thompson approved the constitution.
profile: Jim Haynes was one of three candidates, with Leonard Heydt and John Lovett, who presented their views to the Herald in the race for the first presidency of the Associated Students in May 1966, days after the student body ratified the new constitution.

Haynes captured the presidency the following week, becoming the first president of the Associated Students of Western Kentucky University. The same issue carried a skeptical editorial titled 'We Do Not Deserve Student Government,' a measure of the doubts his administration set out to answer.
Haynes's term closed in May 1967, when the Herald summed up the government's first year as one of organization, progress and apathy and carried president-elect William Menser's plans for 1967-68.

events.title: President Kelly Thompson approves the constitution
events.body: The proposed constitution of the Associated Students of Western Kentucky University was completed in late March and approved on 1 April. The copy held by WKU Archives is dated 7 April 1966.

events.title: Thompson's approval letter is addressed to committee chair Reed Morgan
events.body: The archived copy of Thompson's approval letter names the organizing committee that drafted the constitution: Reed Morgan as chair, John Lovett as vice chair. Morgan's committee did the drafting; Jim Haynes was elected to lead the government it created six weeks later.

src.label: UA3/3/1, Letter to Organizational Committee for a Western Student Organization, 1 Apr 1966

events.title: Students ratify the constitution, 1,812 to 726
events.body: A four-day referendum. 2,538 students voted - a larger raw turnout than most SGA elections have managed since.

events.title: Jim Haynes elected first president
events.body: Seven weeks from presidential approval to a seated student president. Western Kentucky State College became Western Kentucky University on 16 June, so the university and its student government are almost exactly the same age.

events.title: The new government opens its first full year
events.body: The Herald's first issue of the fall reported the student senate ratifying a government appointment as the Associated Students began their first full academic year. Students had approved the constitution and elected officers the previous spring.

events.title: Doing well, but lacking communication
events.body: Midway through the fall semester the Herald judged that Associated Students leaders were performing well but were failing to communicate with the students they represented. It was the first public report card on the year-old government.

events.title: Two vie for the presidency
events.body: The Herald reported two candidates seeking the Associated Students presidency, with campaigns for the organization's second presidential election set to open the following Monday.

events.title: Swearing-in set for May 10
events.body: The Herald announced that newly elected Associated Student officers would be sworn in on May 10, 1967, completing the organization's first full transfer of leadership.

events.title: First year judged: organization, progress, apathy
events.body: Reviewing the government's first year, the Herald found organization and progress alongside persistent student apathy. The same issue carried president-elect William Menser's plans for 1967-68 and a letter arguing that the Associated Students really worked.

events.title: Dean Keown proposes a budget for the new government
events.body: Dean of Students Charles Keown sent President Kelly Thompson a memo proposing a student fee structure to create a budget for the Associated Student Government. He attached fee models gathered from universities across the South and Midwest.

leaders.name: William Menser
leaders.note: ASG president 1967-68. On 4 April 1968 the Herald reported he 'assumes duties as Regent Board Member' - making him WKU's first student regent, two months after the enabling bill was reported in committee. The seat was non-voting at first.

events.title: WKU sends lobbyists to Frankfort for a student on the Board of Regents
events.body: The same Herald issue carries a tuition increase, a discussion group on major issues before the Associated Student Government and a committee investigating women's dormitory rules. This is the origin of the student regent seat.

events.title: A bill to put a student on the Board of Regents reaches committee
events.body: Reported by Ron Lawrence. Western had sent lobbyists to Frankfort for it earlier that month. The same issue carries students berating dorm rules and a letter headed 'Wanted: Work for Judicial Council'.

events.title: William Menser becomes WKU's first student regent
events.body: Two months after the bill was in committee, the Herald reported that Menser 'assumes duties as Regent Board Member'. The seat carried no vote at first. The same issue opens candidate declarations for the next student government election.

events.title: Bill Straeffer wins the presidency; the Herald calls the election a failure
events.body: The issue reporting Straeffer's win also carries an editorial headed 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference'. Turnout anxiety shows up in the second contested election the organisation ever held.

leaders.name: Reed Morgan
leaders.note: Single-year plate. Sits between Menser and Straeffer, whose election the Herald reported on 9 May 1968 - so Morgan likely finished a partial term or held the seat between elections. The only Reed Morgan found in the archive is a different, earlier role: chair of the organizing committee that received President Kelly Thompson's approval letter for the Associated Students constitution, 1 April 1966 - two years before this plaque entry. No Herald or WKU Timeline coverage connects a Reed Morgan to a 1968-69 SGA office. Left unresolved rather than moved, since the 1966 role (committee chair, pre-election) is not the same office the plaque implies.

sources.label: UA3/3/1, Letter to Organizational Committee for a Western Student Organization, 1 Apr 1966

profile: Reed Morgan chaired the student committee that drew up plans for a campus government in 1965-66. In March 1966, answering critics of the project's pace, Morgan replied in the Herald that the committee was not dragging its feet.

A month before students ratified the constitution, the Herald profiled Morgan as a senior who tripled as Greek editor, debater and government chairman, crediting him as a principal architect of the Associated Students plan. The digitized Herald index shows no student government coverage of Morgan in 1968-69 itself.

leaders.name: Bill Straeffer
leaders.note: Election win reported in the Herald, 9 May 1968, in the same issue as an editorial headed 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference'. The internal election-results memo (mirrored below) gives his exact margin: 1,732 votes to Charles Whitley's 1,098.

sources.label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Results of Election, Ron Beck, 3 May 1968

profile: Straeffer ran for the Associated Students presidency against Charles Whitley in the 2 May 1968 election, the organization's second contested presidential race. He won 1,732 votes to Whitley's 1,098. Terry Gilpin was elected vice president in the same election, beating Bob Van Corbach 1,516 to 1,206. Total turnout was 2,894 votes, about 34 percent of the roughly 8,500-student enrollment - a turnout the Herald's coverage of the result treated as a persistent problem, running an editorial in the same issue headed 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference'.

A year later, the Herald's 8 May 1969 issue carried Straeffer and Gilpin's own review of their year in office, headlined 'Associated Students Produces Year of Advancement,' alongside a companion piece, 'Bill Straeffer, Terry Gilpin Review Their Year with Associated Students.' The archive does not yet hold the article text itself, only its headline and byline (Ellen Bennett), so the specifics of what the administration counted as advancement are not yet confirmed.

Bill Straeffer vied with Charles Whitley for the Associated Student Government presidency in the spring 1968 election, the Herald carrying both hopefuls' ideas before the balloting, in a campaign that also saw Terry Gilpin and Bob Van Corbach contest the vice presidency.
Straeffer won the presidency in the May 1968 vote, and in the same issue the Herald reported the new president making plans for 1968-69.
Closing his term in May 1969, Straeffer and vice president Terry Gilpin reviewed their year with the Associated Students for the Herald, which credited the administration with a year of advancement.

leaders.name: Paul Gerard, III
leaders.note: Two-year plate reading 1968-70, immediately after William Menser took the first student regent seat in April 1968. Almost certainly the second student regent. Early student regents were non-voting 'associate regents', which may explain the longer term. Not yet confirmed as regent. A Paul Gerard did appear on the same 2 May 1968 ballot that elected Straeffer, winning the Junior Class presidency 461 votes to Mike Collins' 277 - circumstantially consistent (a junior in spring 1968 would be positioned for a campus-wide office the next year) but not proof of identity or of the regent seat specifically. Two people can share a name; this is flagged, not merged.

sources.label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Results of Election, Ron Beck, 3 May 1968

profile: Paul Gerard first appeared in the Herald's campus politics coverage in April 1968, when the paper reported him battling Mike Collins for a senior class post in that week's election.

By February 1969 Gerard held the student seat on the Board of Regents, and Herald writer Bruce Tucker profiled him as the student regent. He followed William Menser, who in April 1968 had become the first student to sit with the board.

events.title: Straeffer and Whitley vie for the presidency
events.body: The Herald's pre-election coverage set out the field: Bill Straeffer against Charles Whitley for president, Terry Gilpin against Bob Van Corbach for vice president, and contested races down to secretary, treasurer, and congressman at large.

events.title: Straeffer elected president, 1,732 to 1,098; turnout 34 percent
events.body: The Associated Students' internal election-results memo lists the full slate: Bill Straeffer over Charles Whitley for president, Terry Gilpin over Bob Van Corbach for vice president, Becky Cooper over Mary Miller for secretary, Tonii Rizzo over John Combs for treasurer, and John Cobelli and Janie Heathcoat elected congressmen at large over Billy Goodman and Scott Phillips. Total turnout was 2,894 votes, about 34 percent of enrollment.

events.title: Straeffer and Gilpin review their year
events.body: The Herald ran the outgoing administration's own account of its year under the headline 'Associated Students Produces Year of Advancement,' alongside a companion piece on Straeffer and Gilpin reviewing their term.

events.title: Committees go to work
events.body: The Herald reported Associated Students committees swinging into action as the year began. The same issue noted that booking problems still plagued the group's entertainment calendar.

events.title: Judicial Council begins hearing cases
events.body: The Associated Students Judicial Council was hearing student cases, the Herald reported, an early exercise of the judicial power the young government claimed under its constitution.

events.title: Bringing speakers and shows to the Hill
events.body: The Herald reported the Associated Students working to bring speakers and entertainment to campus, alongside notice of an upcoming Associated Students dance.

events.title: A buffer against campus turmoil
events.body: As campus unrest spread nationally, the Herald suggested the Associated Student Government could deter turmoil at Western. The same issue reported president Bill Straeffer moving to discontinue the Greek-oriented Campus Favorites election.

events.title: Paul Gerard profiled as student regent
events.body: Herald writer Bruce Tucker profiled student regent Paul Gerard, and the paper reported a committee appointed to study revision of the Associated Students constitution.

events.title: Election Tuesday as declarations continue
events.body: Declarations of candidacy continued as the Associated Students election was set for the following Tuesday.

events.title: Zielke and Porter outline the coming year
events.body: Incoming leaders Larry Zielke and David Porter outlined the coming Associated Students administration for the Herald, closing the 1968-69 transition.

leaders.name: Paul Gerard, III
leaders.note: Second year of the two-year 1968-70 plate; see 1968-69.
profile: Paul Gerard entered 1969-70 as the sitting student regent, the role in which the Herald had profiled him in February 1969. The student seat still carried no vote.

The limits of the position defined the year around him: in March 1970 the Herald reported the legislature dropping the bill that would have given student regents a vote, under the headline that lawmakers had kept students impotent.

leaders.name: Larry Zielke
leaders.note: Plaque reads 1970-71, paired with John Lyne. Herald coverage places Zielke's actual term here, in 1969-70: he and Frank Genzianelli 'clash for the presidency' in the 25 March 1969 special election edition, and by 22 May 1969 the Herald reports Zielke and running mate David Porter outlining their incoming administration - the term that would open that fall. Lyne, who lost the companion 'second spot' race to Porter in the same 1969 election, went on to win the presidency unopposed in March 1970 for 1970-71 (see that year). The plaque's 1970-71 pairing of Lyne and Zielke conflates two separate one-year terms.
profile: Zielke won the Associated Students presidency in the 25 March 1969 election, beating Frank Genzianelli. David Porter won the companion vice-presidential race the same day, beating John Lyne - the two men who would face each other for the presidency the following year. By 22 May 1969 the Herald was running Zielke and Porter's own outline of their coming administration, in the same issue that covered President Kelly Thompson's resignation announcement.

The plaque records this term one year late, under 1970-71 and paired with Lyne - who did not take office until the following spring. What the Zielke-Porter administration did in office beyond the year-opening outline is not yet confirmed from the archive.

events.title: Genzianelli and Zielke clash for the presidency
events.body: The Herald's Associated Students election special edition covered a two-way presidential race between Frank Genzianelli and Larry Zielke, and a separate race for the second officer spot between John Lyne and David Porter.

events.title: Zielke and Porter outline the coming administration
events.body: With Larry Zielke elected president and David Porter as his second officer, the Herald ran their plans for the 1969-70 Associated Students administration. The same issue covered President Kelly Thompson's resignation announcement.

events.title: Associated Student Congress endorses the Vietnam Moratorium
events.body: The Herald called it a bold step. The clearest early example of the body taking a position outside the campus fence - the same argument that returns in 2017 and 2023.

events.title: Students start grading the faculty
events.body: An ASG committee compiled the results of Western's first student teacher-evaluation effort. The Herald had already editorialised demanding the tabulation move faster.

events.title: 'Associate' regents want voting power
events.body: Two pieces in one issue: Associated Students seeking voting rights for the student regent, and student and faculty 'associate' regents pressing for a vote. An editorial calls for broad support of Senate Bill 75. Two years in, the seat was still symbolic.

events.title: President Kelly Thompson announces his resignation
events.body: Thompson, who had approved the Associated Students constitution in 1966, announced he would step down as WKU's president. The Herald covered it in the same issue as the incoming Zielke-Porter student administration.

events.title: New constitution sent back for study
events.body: The Associated Student Government returned its proposed new constitution for further study while limiting how long the review could run. The same issue reported the group enlisting merchants for a student discount plan.

events.title: ASG urges a probe of student housing
events.body: The Associated Student Government urged an investigation of student housing, one of the fall's most pointed challenges to university policy.

events.title: Congress joins the fight against the superboard
events.body: The Associated Students Congress joined the fight against a proposed state superboard for higher education, and the Herald's editorial page argued the same week that the student regent deserved a vote.

events.title: Lyne wins the presidency before the race begins
events.body: John Lyne won the Associated Students presidency before the race began, his bid unopposed. The same issue reported the legislature dropping the bill that would have given student regents a vote, under a headline that lawmakers had kept students impotent.

events.title: Four constitution changes go to a vote
events.body: The Associated Students Congress moved to seek ratification of four constitution changes, and the Herald saluted vice president David Porter as the government's unsung hero.

events.title: ASG figures in the Kent State week delegations
events.body: During the Strike Western! demonstrations after the Kent State shootings, John Lyne and Larry Zielke were among the students who presented resolutions to President Dero Downing and Dean Charles Keown on May 8, and both sat with the group that received the university's response on May 11.

events.title: Congress endorses Downing's reply to protesters
events.body: As the Strike Western! week wound down, the Associated Student Congress unanimously endorsed President Dero Downing's reply to the protesters, aligning the elected student government with the administration's answer to the demonstrations.

leaders.name: John Lyne
leaders.note: Ran for the Associated Students' second officer spot against David Porter in the 1969 election and lost; won the presidency outright in the 1970 election, unopposed, for the 1970-71 term. The plaque's pairing with Larry Zielke under 1970-71 is wrong - Zielke's term was 1969-70; see that year.

sources.label: Herald 49:35, 13 Mar 1970 - "John Lyne Wins Presidency Before Race Begins"

profile: Lyne first ran for Associated Students office in the March 1969 election, contesting the vice-presidential ('second spot') race against David Porter and losing; Porter went on to serve as Larry Zielke's vice president for 1969-70. A year later, no one filed against Lyne for the 1970-71 presidency, and the Herald reported on 13 March 1970 that he had 'won the presidency before the race begins.' Doug Alexander won the vice presidency the same election cycle, beating Steve Tichenor, in a vote held the following week.

The term began against the backdrop of the Kent State shootings that May: the Associated Student Congress's October 1970 resolution on the women's curfew ran in a Herald issue whose letters page was dominated by students arguing about Kent State, and the same fall the Board of Regents seated eight students on the Academic Council. What Lyne's administration itself proposed or passed beyond the curfew resolution is not yet confirmed from the archive.

John Lyne was one of the most visible students on the Hill before taking office, writing a steady stream of Herald columns through 1969-70 and representing Kentuckians in the national draft lottery drawing in December 1969.
Lyne won the Associated Students presidency in March 1970 without opposition, the Herald reporting that he had captured the office before the race began.

Through 1970-71 Lyne fought his administration's corner in the Herald's letters column, complaining in January that he had been kept in the dark about an appointment and defending the Associated Students lecture series against attack that April, in the issue that reported W.S. Moss taking the oath as regent.

events.title: John Lyne wins the presidency before the race begins
events.body: No opponent filed against Lyne for the 1970-71 Associated Students presidency, and the Herald reported him elected without a contest.

events.title: Doug Alexander captures the vice presidency
events.body: Alexander beat Steve Tichenor for the Associated Students vice presidency in the vote held the week after Lyne's uncontested presidential win.

events.title: Regents seat eight students on the Academic Council
events.body: An editorial framed it as the Regents opening doors to student expression in academics. Representation was arriving faster in the curriculum committees than on the board itself.

events.title: A resolution on the women's curfew, five months after Kent State
events.body: The Associated Student Congress passed a curfew resolution; the Herald reported abolition was unlikely that year and editorialised that the curfew was obsolete. The letters page in the same issue is almost entirely students arguing about Kent State.

events.title: A committee opens a constitution study
events.body: A committee was formed to study Associated Student constitutions, renewing the reform effort that had produced a second constitution the year before.

events.title: Resolutions pass; a center for students sought
events.body: Resolutions gained approval in the Associated Students Congress, and the government pressed its call for a center for students in the Herald's pages.

events.title: Twenty offices go begging
events.body: With filing open for the spring elections, the Herald reported twenty student government offices going begging for candidates.

events.title: Eighty-four to seek campus offices
events.body: By election eve the field had filled out: the Herald counted 84 students seeking campus offices in Tuesday's voting.

events.title: Linda Jones elected first woman president
events.body: Linda Jones was elected the first woman president of the Associated Student Government. The Western Alumnus pictured her being sworn in alongside faculty regent Lowell Harrison.

src.label: WKU Timeline: Linda Jones (Western Alumnus, 6 Apr 1971)

events.title: New congress leaders air the issues
events.body: The newly elected Associated Student Congress leaders aired major issues for the Herald and gave clues on what to expect in the fall.

executive.name: John Lyne
executive.note: Unopposed.

executive.name: Doug Alexander
executive.note: Beat Steve Tichenor.

leaders.name: Linda Jones
leaders.note: First woman to hold the office. The Herald of 28 April 1972 carries a piece headed 'Jones, Linda. Reflects on Term' in the same issue as a strike call over dorm visitation.

events.title: Associated Students affiliates with a wider student association
events.body: An early attempt to gain leverage beyond the Hill. Which body it joined is not clear from the article index alone.

events.title: 'Student Regent May Get Vote'
events.body: Four years after the seat was created it was still non-voting. The same issue has the Academic Council clarifying grievance procedure and an Associated Students open session scheduled for 12 February.

events.title: 'Chaos Reigns at Associated Students Meeting'
events.body: The same issue carries students planning a petition to force dorm visitation and a separate piece arguing student interest had collapsed and the Associated Students had followed it down.

events.title: A strike threat over visitation, and six votes won on a university council
events.body: A Mass Action Committee called for a strike over dorm visitation while the Associated Students installed next year's officers. Buried in the same issue: students gained six votes on a university council. Linda Jones reflected on her term.

leaders.name: Edward Jordan, Jr.
leaders.note: Paired on the plaque with Michael Fiorella, who is confirmed as the student regent that year - so Jordan is the president by elimination. Confirm with April 1972 Herald election coverage.
profile: Edward Jordan's name entered the Herald's letters columns on November 7, 1972, when he and Charles Boteler urged readers to restore ideals. The digitized index does not label the ASG office Jordan held.
On April 10, 1973, as top ASG offices went on the line in the spring election, a letter praising Ed Jordan ran in the Herald.
Jordan stayed in student politics after his year: in April 1974 he wrote to the Herald judging Steve Henry the most qualified candidate in that spring's races.

leaders.name: Michael Fiorella
leaders.note: Student regent, not president. Sworn in 26 September 1972 alongside gubernatorial appointees Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry, who Gov. Wendell Ford had named the previous month.
profile: In September 1972 the Herald profiled Michael Fiorella, the Associated Student Government vice president, under the headline that he was anti-apathy.
A week later the Herald reported that Fiorella had won the student seat on the Board of Regents.
Fiorella was sworn in on September 26, 1972, alongside Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry, the board's two other new members.

events.title: Gov. Wendell Ford names two regents
events.body: Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry. The same issue reports the best ASG course evaluation yet, students questioning the $5 car registration fee, and filing opening for ASG offices.

events.title: Three new regents sworn in, one of them a student
events.body: Michael Fiorella took the student seat alongside Edds and Embry. The same issue reports 'Slack Time at Associated Student Government Congress', an ASG bankruptcy plan and the open-dorm visitation fight continuing.

events.title: A year of involvement promised
events.body: The Herald opened the year reporting Associated Student Government plans for a year of involvement, in an issue that also covered the regents approving a five dollar vehicle registration fee.

events.title: Course evaluation called the best yet
events.body: The Herald judged ASG's course evaluation the best yet, as filing opened for fall ASG offices.

events.title: Five file for student regent; cheerleader ruling deplored
events.body: Five students filed for the student seat on the Board of Regents. In the same issue, an ASG resolution deplored a cheerleader ruling as the university bowed to Black students' demands after a bitter squabble over squad selection.

events.title: Funds fly as Chicago is booked
events.body: ASG funds flew as the group set a Chicago concert, corrected a tactical error by adding more polls to a campus vote, and made its student activity card available.

events.title: Fiorella wins the regent seat
events.body: Michael Fiorella, the Associated Student Government vice president, won the student seat on the Board of Regents. Days earlier the Herald had profiled him as anti-apathy.

events.title: ASG rejects Downing's position on Black affairs
events.body: The Associated Student Government rejected President Dero Downing's position on an Office of Black Affairs, one of the sharpest confrontations of the fall. A congressman's letter the same day called criticism of ASG unjustified.

events.title: Students as campus cops
events.body: ASG wanted students serving as campus police, the Herald reported, while the editorial page argued more time was needed between elections.

events.title: Top offices on the line
events.body: Top Associated Student Government offices went on the line in the day's election, and a letter writer praised Ed Jordan as the voting opened.

leaders.name: Steven Yater
leaders.note: No name is listed for 1974-75 as a single term; the next two plates both read 1974-75. Sole name on the plaque for this year and no competing entry, so almost certainly the president. Not yet confirmed against Herald election coverage.
profile: Steve Yater led the Associated Student Government through 1973-74. Early in his term he publicly commended the Board of Regents in the Herald, weeks after the board had increased ASG's budget allotment.
In April 1974, stung by election-season criticism, President Yater defended his administration in a letter to the Herald.
His final weeks in office stayed argumentative: the Herald of April 30 carried dueling letters under the heading 'Linda Jones vs. Steven Yater' as the student regent race closed out the year.

events.title: Gregory McKinney sworn in as WKU's first African American student regent
events.body: Seven years before Julius Price became the first Black gubernatorial appointee to the board in 1981. The student seat integrated the Board of Regents first.

events.title: Regents raise the ASG allotment
events.body: The Herald opened the year reporting a budget bulge: the Board of Regents voted to increase the Associated Student Government allotment. A companion piece introduced freshmen to ASG under the headline 'Every College Has One.'

events.title: Free University continues, smaller
events.body: ASG's Free University of no-cost, no-credit evening courses continued for another year, though with fewer courses than before.

events.title: Housing survey urges dorm improvements
events.body: An ASG housing survey urged improvement in dormitory conditions, part of a fall agenda that also included a committee on part-time student opportunities and a push for paper recycling.

events.title: A congressman resigns in protest
events.body: ASG representative Reginald Glass resigned his post in protest, the Herald reported, an early sign of strain inside the congress.

events.title: Sam Ervin booked for April
events.body: ASG contracted Senator Sam Ervin, chairman of the Senate Watergate committee, to speak at Western on April 2. The same issue reported ASG acting to revamp its committees.

events.title: Spending limit stays
events.body: ASG voted to retain its campaign spending limit rather than loosen the cap on campaign outlays.

events.title: Consolo and Henry win the election
events.body: Jeff Consolo and Steve Henry won the spring ASG election, in a cycle whose primary the Herald said showed Greek influence. Henry resigned his post over the student discount program after the results.

events.title: Five file for the student regent seat
events.body: Five students filed for the student seat on the Board of Regents ahead of the spring vote, the position that carried a place at the board table.

leaders.name: Gregory McKinney
leaders.note: Student regent, not president. Sworn in 19 June 1974 as WKU's first African American student regent.

sources.label: WKU Timeline: Gregory McKinney (Western Alumnus, 19 Jun 1974)

profile: Gregory McKinney came to campus prominence as a speaker: in March 1974 the Herald reported him winning top honors in competition.

That spring McKinney ran for the student seat on the Board of Regents against Sid Stevens, the two candidates' final appeals running side by side in the Herald as an editorial called the race a clear choice for voters.
McKinney won the seat and was sworn in on June 19, 1974, becoming WKU's first African American student regent.

leaders.name: Jeffrey Consolo
leaders.note: ASG president. The Herald of 1974 reports 'Jeff Consolo Tabs Eight for Congress' - a president making appointments to the Associated Student Congress.
profile: Jeff Consolo won the Associated Student Government presidency in the March 1974 election on a ticket with Steve Henry, in a cycle whose primary the Herald said showed Greek influence.
Taking office, Consolo told the Herald he hoped for increased student involvement during his term.

Consolo's term closed on April 15, 1975, when new ASG officers were installed at the day's meeting after a spring in which his congress had simplified election procedures and wound down its concert program.

events.title: Regents extend visitation as the year opens
events.body: The Herald's opening issue reported the Board of Regents extending dormitory visitation and approving a $29.8 million budget at the board's first session of the year.

events.title: Voting procedures simplified for the spring election
events.body: ASG passed a motion simplifying voting procedures for the spring election, and the ASG treasurer took to the Herald's letters column the same day.

events.title: New officers installed; concert plans dropped
events.body: New Associated Student Government officers were installed at the day's meeting, as the outgoing congress abandoned plans for a final concert of the semester and the editorial page pronounced incoming president Steve Henry's entertainment plan inadequate.

leaders.name: Steve Henry
leaders.note: Check whether this is the Steve Henry who later served as Lieutenant Governor of Kentucky (1995-2003). Do not assert the identification without a source.
profile: Steve Henry appeared in ASG coverage as early as September 1972, when the Herald reported his view that the Associated Student Government had lost respect.
Henry won the spring 1974 election on a ticket with Jeff Consolo, and resigned his post running the student discount program after the victory.

As president in 1975-76 Henry moved in November to change ASG's concert proposal after a money-losing fall season, while a student group urged support for his energy awareness plan. At year's end the Herald summed up his tenure with a piece on how the role had required balancing the twin jobs of student regent and ASG president, which he held at the same time.

events.title: Big concert, big loss
events.body: An ASG concert drew 4,300 people but lost $7,000, the Herald reported, opening a money argument that ran through the fall.

events.title: ASG suggests a campus bank
events.body: ASG suggested creating a campus bank for students, one of the new administration's early service proposals.

events.title: Budget approved amid concert debate
events.body: The ASG budget won approval as concerts were discussed, two weeks after the money-losing season opener had put the program under scrutiny.

events.title: Fund misuse charges aired
events.body: Charges of ASG fund misuse were heard in the same week the congress voted to create an activities committee and a letter writer attacked the organization.

events.title: A budget remedy and a book exchange
events.body: The Herald weighed whether a new ASG budget offered a remedy, and reported a spring semester book exchange to be co-sponsored by ASG and Veterans on Campus. President Steve Henry moved to change the concert proposal the same week.

events.title: Petition drive seeks support
events.body: ASG sought student support with a petition and prepared to hear appeals over its concert policy as the fall semester closed.

events.title: Election season and an acquittal
events.body: During the spring election season ASG acquitted congress member Gerard Faulk in an internal proceeding, and the Herald polled voters on the races.

events.title: Final meeting approves a budget
events.body: The congress approved a tentative budget at the final ASG meeting of the year, and the Herald assessed how Steve Henry's year had required balancing his twin jobs as student regent and ASG president.

leaders.name: Christy Mollozzi
leaders.note: The outgoing president who 'congratulates voters' in the 15 April 1977 Herald is Christy Vogt, and a Christy Vogt letter dated 26 April 1977 sits in the SGA document series. Vogt and Mollozzi are very likely the same person under maiden and married names. Confirm before merging.

events.title: Bob Moore elected ASG president by 26 votes
events.body: One of the narrowest margins in the record. The same issue carries the outgoing president congratulating voters, the faculty asking for a say in hiring, and Western fighting a beer licence for a local pizzeria.

events.title: ASG creates constitutional revision committee
events.body: The Associated Student Government congress passed Bill 2, creating a committee charged with revising the organization's constitution. Constitutional revision remained on the ASG agenda for the rest of the school year and appeared again among proposed amendments and a spring referendum bill.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Bill 2 - Constitutional Revision Committee, 7 Sep 1976

events.title: ASG asks WKU for a student minimum wage
events.body: The congress adopted Resolution 13, proposing that Western institute a minimum wage policy for all student employees. It was part of a heavy fall docket that also included resolutions on parking, laundry services, non-smoking areas and residence hall change machines.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Resolution 13 - Minimum Wage, 26 Oct 1976

events.title: Seals and Crofts concert loses ASG $3,800
events.body: The Herald reported that the Seals and Crofts concert set the Associated Student Government back $3,800. Concert finances would remain a recurring sore point for ASG through the rest of the decade.

events.title: ASG recommends preregistration for all students
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG would recommend preregistration for all students. Advance registration was one of the four items president Christy Vogt later carried into her end-of-year recommendations to the administration.

events.title: Discrimination resolution fails as 14 abstain
events.body: Fourteen members abstained as the Associated Student Government rejected a resolution on discrimination, the Herald reported. The same issue noted that filing for ASG posts would begin the following Monday.

events.title: ASG passes bill opposing tuition increase
events.body: The congress approved Bill 9, formally opposing a proposed tuition increase. The same March meeting produced Bill 8, which created a Complaint Committee to handle student grievances.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Bill 9 - Opposition to Tuition Increase, 8 Mar 1977

events.title: Vogt closes the congress with four recommendations
events.body: President Christy Vogt sent a letter closing the congress and thanking ASG members for their work. She left four items to recommend to the administration: constitutional revision, extended hours for student buildings, open visitation and advanced registration.

src.label: SGA Records (UA66), Christy Vogt Letter, 26 Apr 1977

leaders.name: Robert Moore
leaders.note: Elected ASG president by a 26-vote margin, reported 15 April 1977. Herald bylines call him 'Bob Moore.'
profile: Moore entered the 1977 Associated Student Government presidential race against Tom Blair. The Herald's April 8 issue set up the contest alongside the treasurer's race between George Carlson and rivals; four days later Mark McChesney's letter backing Moore ran alongside endorsements for the rest of the ticket, as outgoing president Christy Vogt urged students to get involved.

Moore won on April 15, 1977, by 26 votes over Blair - one of the narrowest presidential margins in the record - in an issue that also carried the faculty asking for a say in hiring and Western fighting a beer licence for a local pizzeria.

That October, as president, Moore publicly questioned how freshman candidates in that fall's class elections were spending their campaign money. The comment drew enough pushback that the Herald ran an editorial the same week headlined 'Bob Moore's Comment Isn't Good Politics.'

The archive does not yet show what Moore's administration did over the winter and into the spring beyond the ordinary business of readying his succession - see the 1978 election events below. By September 1978, after his term had ended, the Herald reported that Moore had been found ineligible for another Associated Student Government job; the archive does not yet hold the article's account of why.

events.title: Moore questions freshman candidates' campaign spending
events.body: President Bob Moore publicly questioned how freshman class candidates were spending their campaign money. The Herald ran an editorial the same week, 'Bob Moore's Comment Isn't Good Politics,' pushing back on his remark.

events.title: Spending limits set for the coming ASG election
events.body: The Associated Student Government set spending limits for candidates ahead of the spring election that would choose Moore's successor.

events.title: Thornton and Johnson contest the presidency; four offices go uncontested
events.body: Steve Thornton and Ed Johnson faced off for the Associated Student Government presidency, Thornton campaigning on his experience, while four other offices had no opponent on the ballot.

events.title: Johnson contests his loss to Thornton
events.body: Ed Johnson, having lost the presidential race, contested the Associated Student Government election result.

events.title: Judicial Council denies Johnson's appeal
events.body: After a long debate, the Associated Student Government Judicial Council denied Ed Johnson's appeal of the election result, letting Steve Thornton's win stand.

leaders.name: Steven Thornton
leaders.note: Contested the ASG presidency against Ed Johnson in the 6 April 1978 election, campaigning on his experience; Johnson's contest of the result was denied by the Judicial Council on 18 April 1978 (see 1977-78 events, the outgoing Moore administration's year). This replaces a prior citation to 'Herald 54:54, 12 Apr 1979' - that issue is the following year's primary, does not name Thornton, and has been moved to 1979-80.

leaders.name: James Hargroave
leaders.note: Surname spelling on the plaque is HARGROAVE. The Herald, in a 30 August 1979 profile calling him ASG Head at the start of the year, spells the name 'Jamie Hargrove.' Flagging the discrepancy rather than silently correcting the plaque spelling, per project rule.
profile: By August 30, 1979, at the start of the school year, the Herald profiled the Associated Student Government head - spelled 'Jamie Hargrove' in the byline - under the headline that he believed students were interested. The archive does not yet hold the spring 1979 election coverage that put him in office; see the events below for the primary that preceded it.

The archive does not yet show what Hargrove's administration passed or fought over during 1979-80 beyond the record's general sweep of the year. Further Herald issues from the fall and spring semester have not yet been checked.

events.title: 830 students vote in the ASG primary; the Herald runs a defence of not voting
events.body: The Associated Student Government's spring primary drew 830 voters and put the open-house policy on the ballot. The same issue carried a piece justifying student apathy in ASG voting - the paper had moved from scolding non-voters to explaining them. This primary elected the officers who took office for 1979-80; it was previously misfiled under 1978-79.

events.title: Donald Zacharias sworn in as WKU's sixth president
events.body: Zacharias, previously executive assistant to the chancellor of the University of Texas system, took office as WKU's sixth president at the opening of the academic year; he was formally installed the following spring.

events.title: ASG head Jamie Hargrove profiled at year's start
events.body: The Herald profiled the Associated Student Government head under the headline that he believed students were interested, in the same issue that introduced the new president's wife, Tommie Zacharias, to campus.

events.title: ASG weighs expanding hall representation
events.body: The Associated Student Government considered expanding residence hall representation in its congress, in the same issue reporting the Board of Regents set to consider a two-year budget request.

events.title: Resolution 79-10 seeks staff for scholarship administration
events.body: The Associated Student Government passed Resolution 79-10, urging the university to assign staff to administer academic scholarships.

events.title: ASG proposes a title change
events.body: The Associated Student Government proposed a title change for the organization. The proposal surfaced in the same week campus activities were limited for the national election day.

events.title: ASG asks the state to evaluate higher education
events.body: ASG asked the state to evaluate higher education. The request came in a legislative season dominated by budget worries across Kentucky's universities.

events.title: Sturgeon and Bush win the ASG primary
events.body: David Sturgeon and Marcel Bush won the Associated Student Government primary, in a campaign the Herald said saw candidates playing big time politics. The same issue carried a resolution asking for a new ASG logo.

events.title: Bush defeats Sturgeon for the presidency
events.body: David Sturgeon was defeated in the Associated Student Government race, leaving Marcel Bush the winner after endorsements had split between the two. The congress also voted to keep the present ASG logo.

events.title: Close races prompt ASG recounts
events.body: Close races prompted recounts in the Associated Student Government election. The recounts came in the same week the Council on Higher Education approved a tuition increase.

events.title: ASG changes its mind on changing minds
events.body: The Herald reported that the Associated Student Government changed its mind on changing minds, capping a contentious election month. The same issue covered a withdrawn regent selection and the board's study of reorganizing the university.

events.title: Sandra Norfleet elected student regent
events.body: Reported by Kevin Francke. The same issue has a group set to speak on the Associated Student Government's behalf and Western's 1982 budget coming off hold.

events.title: ASG announces its goals for the year
events.body: The Associated Student Government announced its goals for the coming year. Within two weeks its executives were defending their actions in the Herald, whose editorial page complained that petty politics plagued the organization.

events.title: Campaign spending limit raised
events.body: ASG voted to increase its campaign spending limit. The change followed a week of debate over whether the cap should rise.

events.title: ASG vetoes plan to pay an education lobbyist
events.body: The Associated Student Government vetoed a plan to pay an education lobbyist. The vote came weeks after ASG had rallied publicly for higher education funding.

events.title: ASG appoints a council to decide disputes
events.body: ASG appointed a council to decide internal disputes. The same issue reported that the regents bill, changing how the student regent was chosen, had passed the state House.

events.title: Five students seek the student regent seat
events.body: Five students sought the student regent spot in the first campus-wide election for the seat. The February 9 vote produced no majority, forcing a runoff the following week.

events.title: Ragan and Sargent survive the presidential primary
events.body: Margaret Ragan and Glenn Sargent survived the Associated Student Government presidential primary. The field had included Jack Smith, Kerrie Stewart and Jack Murphree, whose supporters filled the Herald's letters pages.

events.title: General election results voided
events.body: The student government election results were voided, a decision the Herald said disgusted the candidates. A repeat general election was scheduled for April 20.

events.title: Margaret Ragan wins the repeated election
events.body: Margaret Ragan won the ASG presidency in the repeated general election. The new officers were sworn in the following week.

leaders.name: David Payne
leaders.note: One of three names attached to 1982. Likely a mid-year succession.
profile: David Payne first appears in the indexed record in February 1981 with a Herald letter titled 'Apathy Erased'. By October 1981 he was writing on the Associated Student Government's behalf, declaring that ASG was rallying for higher education as budget cuts loomed.

In early February 1982 the Herald reported that Payne wanted another adviser for ASG, and its editorial page attacked his judgment, while a report the next week said Payne considered certain resolutions misdirected. The indexed headlines identify him as ASG's leading spokesman that winter but do not state his office.

Later that month, letter writers to the Herald argued that Payne had been made a victim in the affair. His name does not appear in the indexed headlines of the spring 1982 election that chose Margaret Ragan, nor in the 1982-83 issues examined.

leaders.name: Sandra Norfleet
leaders.note: Student regent, not president. Election reported in the Herald, 18 February 1982.
profile: No candidate won a majority on February 9, forcing a runoff, which Norfleet won on February 16. The Herald reported her election as student regent in its February 18 issue.

Her initial term was short: by mid-April 1982 the Herald noted that the student regent's 2-month term was nearing its end. She is listed among the 1982-83 student leaders, and in February 1983 the Herald's editorial page was still weighing the office, insisting the student regent must represent everyone.

leaders.name: Margaret Ragan
profile: Margaret Ragan survived the April 1982 Associated Student Government presidential primary along with Glenn Sargent, emerging from a five-way field. Endorsement letters for her ran in the Herald through both rounds of the election.
After the first general election was voided, Ragan won the presidency in the repeated election held April 20, 1982. She and the other new officers were sworn in before the month was out.

Midway through her term Ragan used the Herald's pages to explain that the ASG presidency and the student regent seat were now separate positions. Her spring saw a grade plan, a student shuttle vote, and a contested rewrite of the ASG constitution before Jack Smith was elected to succeed her.

events.title: Ragan: ASG presidency and student regent are separate jobs
events.body: President Margaret Ragan wrote in the Herald that the Associated Student Government presidency and the student regent position were separate. The distinction reflected the 1982 change that made the student regent directly elected by the student body.

events.title: Grade plan passes; students vote for a shuttle
events.body: ASG passed a grade plan, and 206 students voted for a campus shuttle service. The shuttle idea drew an offer of help from the TVA two weeks later.

events.title: Constitution changes approved; filing opens
events.body: The Associated Student Government approved changes to its constitution, and ten students filed for offices ahead of the deadline. Dean Charles Keown publicly questioned the revisions the following week, as filings swelled to 68.

events.title: 500 vote in the ASG primary
events.body: About 500 students voted in the Associated Student Government primary. The Herald's letters pages carried a steady stream of endorsements for presidential candidate Jack Smith.

events.title: Jack Smith wins the ASG presidency
events.body: Jack Smith won the presidency of the Associated Student Government, and students voted for the ASG constitutional revisions on the same ballot. The Herald had dared students to vote at all in a sardonic election day editorial.

events.title: ASG endorses a $15 athletic fee
events.body: The outgoing congress endorsed a $15 athletic fee. The vote came as the Board of Regents turned its focus to the budget.

leaders.name: Jack Smith
leaders.note: Two-year plate. Either re-elected or the plaque compresses two terms.
profile: Jack Smith first ran for the Associated Student Government presidency in spring 1982, drawing repeated endorsement letters in the Herald, and though Margaret Ragan won that race, Smith and Lonnie Sears took awards as the year closed. He returned as a candidate in March 1983, when 68 students filed for ASG positions and his supporters again filled the letters pages.

Smith won the presidency of the Associated Student Government in the April 12, 1983 election, in which students also approved constitutional revisions. His victory came after roughly 500 students had voted in the primary the week before.

His presidency was colorful and contentious: the fall brought a discount card controversy, letters accusing him of partying while committees waited and others defending him, and a December cartoon that he wrote in to protest. In April 1984 the Herald caught him impersonating a bunny as his ASG ran a low-turnout poll on beer and a campus pub.

events.title: Escort service returns; discount card floated
events.body: The Herald's opening issue reported that the student escort service would resume and that ASG might sponsor a discount card. Filing for freshman elections was set to begin September 19.

events.title: Discount card plan draws fire
events.body: ASG voted to study the discount card after the Herald editorialized that the organization should govern, not market cards. A week later the paper reported ASG would offer members a commission on card sales, prompting letters calling the plan cheap shots and old tricks.

events.title: ASG passes incomplete-grade deadline proposal
events.body: The Associated Student Government passed its proposal on the deadline for incomplete grades, after tabling it the week before. The grade issue had occupied ASG since September.

events.title: ASG voids its own procedures amid growth
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG voided its own procedures, while also noting growth in membership and a congress weighing 14 proposals. The editorial page mocked the body with a cartoon, and Jack Smith wrote in to say the cartoon aggravated him.

events.title: Student legislature may rejoin ASG
events.body: The Kentucky Student Legislature delegation was reported possibly rejoining the Associated Student Government. Letter writers sparred the same day over whether the ASG stereotype was deserved.

events.title: Top four ASG offices decided without runoffs
events.body: The top four Associated Student Government spots were decided, the Herald reported, as ASG emphasized representation. About 450 students had voted in the primary the week before.

events.title: ASG polls students on beer and a campus pub
events.body: ASG began a student poll on the beer and campus pub issue on general election day. The Herald's editorial page argued the economics of the campus pub plan were faulty.

events.title: Low turnout may force a beer poll revote
events.body: Low turnout threatened to spur a revote in the ASG beer poll. The same issue reported president Jack Smith impersonating a bunny for the season.

leaders.name: Jack Smith
leaders.note: Two-year plate. Either re-elected or the plaque compresses two terms.
profile: Smith presided over a productive opening to the 1984-85 year. By the third week of September the Herald reported that four ASG proposals had been made reality, and the congress had begun studying a student book exchange, which became the signature project of his final year.
By mid-year the record was mixed. The book exchange venture appeared likely to take a summer pause, and the organization was weighing whether to fight cuts to education funding.

His term ended in April 1985. The Herald covered his exit with a news story headlined that Smith was ending his term as ASG president, an editorial crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organization, and an editorial cartoon. The SGA plaque records him on a two-year 1983-85 plate.

events.title: Apathy as an editorial cartoon
events.body: 'Voter Apathy Can be Solved' ran alongside a cartoon on election apathy and a report that a 24-hour open house was under discussion.

events.title: Four proposals made reality in the third week of class
events.body: The Herald reported that four Associated Student Government proposals had already been carried out, and that the congress was beginning a study of a student book exchange. The exchange went on to become the running project of the year.

events.title: The grade scale proposal is denied
events.body: ASG's proposal for a new grade scale was denied, one week after the congress's early run of successes. It was the first setback of the fall reported in the Herald's coverage.

events.title: ASG wants less general education
events.body: The congress went on record wanting a reduction in general education requirements. It was an early instance of the body intervening in curriculum policy, three years before the fights over the General Education Task Force.

events.title: LaMont Jones drops out of a revote
events.body: LaMont Jones withdrew from an ASG revote, and the same issue carried an editorial cartoon on the organization. A disputed election requiring a revote marked the low point of the fall semester.

events.title: Education cuts loom and the book exchange stalls
events.body: ASG weighed a fight against state education cuts, while its book exchange venture looked likely to pause for the summer. Both stories ran in the same late-January issue.

events.title: Four file for congress president
events.body: A fourth candidate filed for ASG congress president and a debate was set, as the spring filing period opened. The same issue carried letters both applauding an ASG bill and requesting its support.

events.title: McKinney and Watkins take the primary
events.body: Mitchell McKinney and Chris Watkins rode their experience to victory in the ASG primary. The congress also passed a resolution on grade point averages the same week.

events.title: Jack Smith ends his term
events.body: The Herald marked the end of Jack Smith's presidency with a news story, an editorial crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in ASG, and an editorial cartoon. Mitchell McKinney had been elected the new president the week before.

leaders.name: Mitchell McKinney
leaders.note: February 1985 Herald ran an apathy editorial and cartoon plus a report on 24-hour open house discussions.
profile: McKinney won the spring 1985 primary on a ticket with Chris Watkins; the Herald's headline said the pair rode experience to their primary victory.
He was announced as the new Associated Student Government president in the Herald of 4 April 1985, in the same issue that reported a legislative group rejoining ASG.

In March 1986 McKinney pulled out of the race for a second term. The same issue carried a piece arguing that student government needed a strong leader, and the field he left behind grew to four candidates before Tim Todd won the presidency that April. A 1986 presidential proclamation he signed honoring English professor Thomas Jones survives in the SGA records.

events.title: A 20-vote margin and a GPA debate
events.body: About 20 votes separated the top two finishers in a fall ASG election, and the congress debated setting a grade-point average requirement for its own members. Both stories ran in the same late-October issue.

events.title: Alcohol on campus studied again
events.body: ASG returned to the question of alcohol on campus, an issue that had already produced a student poll and a campus pub debate in 1984. The congress opened a new study of the policy.

events.title: A shuttle to the mall
events.body: The congress discussed running a shuttle service from campus to the mall. It was one of several consumer-service ideas, alongside student discount cards, floated that fall.

events.title: Lighting proposal defeated
events.body: Student government defeated a campus lighting proposal in the last week of the fall semester. It was one of the few outright defeats of legislation reported that year.

events.title: Fall-break bill narrowly passes
events.body: A bill calling for a fall break narrowly passed ASG. The proposal drew an opposing editorial in the next issue calling the extra break impractical and not needed.

events.title: No day off for Martin Luther King Day
events.body: ASG rejected a proposal to dismiss classes for the Martin Luther King holiday, one week after passing the fall-break bill. The King holiday question returned to the congress the following year.

events.title: Library hours proposals, and elections delayed a week
events.body: ASG proposals asked for more library hours, and the spring elections were pushed back a week. The same issue carried dueling letters on whether the organization was in trouble.

events.title: Pranks and accusations mar the races
events.body: The Herald reported that pranks and accusations had marred the ASG races, and printed the election results in the same issue. Tim Todd emerged from the field as the new president.

leaders.name: Timothy Todd
leaders.note: Two-year plate. A 1987 Herald piece reports a candidate shortage and mentions a Tim Todd race.
profile: Todd reached the April 1986 runoff against Greg Elder after Mitchell McKinney's withdrawal left the presidential field open. The Herald reported the two-man race on 3 April, with the general election the following week.

Days after an election week the Herald described as marred by pranks and accusations, the paper identified Todd as the new ASG president in a sharply critical opinion piece headlined that he lacked knowledge of his own issues. Todd answered in print the following issue, criticizing the paper's reporting.
His first fall opened with an approved budget of $12,100, a plan to reach students by phone for their ideas and needs, and an ASG retreat featuring university president Kern Alexander.

events.title: Twenty years of amendments consolidated into one document
events.body: The constitution of the WKU Associated Students with amendments - the only surviving snapshot of how the 1966 framework had been patched over two decades. A Judicial Council roster for 1986-87 survives alongside it.

events.title: A $12,100 budget and a retreat with the university president
events.body: ASG approved a $12,100 budget, planned a phone outreach effort to hear students' ideas and needs, and announced a retreat featuring university president Kern Alexander. All three stories ran in the second week of the fall semester.

events.title: A minor change in voting
events.body: ASG sought a minor change in its voting procedures early in the fall term. It was the first structural tinkering of the Todd presidency.

events.title: Rules suspended, bills passed
events.body: The congress suspended its rules to pass a batch of bills in a single meeting. The rush came as the spring filing period for elections was opening.

events.title: Martin Luther King bill splits the congress
events.body: A Martin Luther King bill passed the congress with members split by the argument, a year after ASG had rejected dismissing classes for the holiday. The same issue reported that Tim Todd and Greg Elder would battle again for the presidency.

events.title: Attendance drops after the speeches
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG attendance fell off once campaign speeches had been heard. An accompanying piece warned voters that talk was cheap in the presidential race.

events.title: An amendment dies of low member turnout
events.body: A constitutional amendment was defeated because too few members turned up to vote on it. The failure came in the same week as the presidential election.

events.title: The Herald calls the race for Elder; the index calls it no contest
events.body: On election day the Herald endorsed challenger Greg Elder as the better choice to lead ASG, ran a letter calling the organization impotent, and headlined the race itself as no contest. The indexed issues that survive do not record the published result; the SGA plaque carries Todd through 1988 on a two-year plate.

leaders.name: Timothy Todd
leaders.note: Two-year plate. A 1987 Herald piece reports a candidate shortage and mentions a Tim Todd race.
profile: Todd sought a second term in spring 1987 in a rematch against Greg Elder, the man he had beaten the year before. The Herald reported the two would battle again in its 19 March issue.

On election day the Herald endorsed Elder as the better choice and indexed the race itself under the headline no contest. The surviving indexed issues do not record the published result; the SGA plaque lists Todd on a single 1986-88 plate, and no other president appears in the 1987-88 record.
The 1987-88 year under the two-year plate ended with the election of Scott Whitehouse on 7 April 1988, closing out the era of the Todd presidency.

events.title: Not enough candidates to fill the ballot
events.body: ASG races faced a candidate shortage; one report notes a candidate entered a race to help a rival rather than to win. The same issue has ASG tabling a phone bill after amendment.

events.title: Dropping the intercollegiate legislature considered
events.body: ASG considered dropping its membership in the intercollegiate legislature, while the Herald warned that sharing an officer with Interhall Council could mean trouble for both groups. An editorial the following week argued the Kentucky Intercollegiate State Legislature was worth keeping as a way to promote ideas.

events.title: Crosswalk resolution passes
events.body: The congress passed a resolution calling for a crosswalk. Campus safety items, including new screens for dormitory windows, filled much of the fall agenda.

events.title: Getting tough on absenteeism
events.body: ASG moved to get tough on absenteeism after a member lost his seat the week before. The Herald was simultaneously reporting that apathy was killing both ASG and the Residence Hall Association.

events.title: Constitutional amendments up for a vote
events.body: Constitutional amendments went before the body in November, in the same season the congress was pushing for required teacher evaluations. It was the third straight year of structural revision attempts.

events.title: ASG explains its empty seats
events.body: The organization publicly cited its reasons for the vacancies in its ranks, and four congress positions had been filled at a single meeting earlier that month. Days later an editorial told the body it needed better ideas, not gimmicks.

events.title: Ragland and Whitehouse win the primaries
events.body: Shannon Ragland and Scott Whitehouse won the ASG presidential primaries, narrowing a field of seven. The same issue reported passage of a proposal requesting a memorial area on campus.

events.title: Whitehouse elected; condom machines approved
events.body: Scott Whitehouse won the ASG presidential election, in an issue that also reported the congress approving condom machines for campus. The election coverage ran alongside editorials saying oversight and closed minds had marred the process.

events.title: Bruce Cambron calls for a new election
events.body: Bruce Cambron called for a new election a week after the results, following coverage of votes cast for a write-in candidate that ASG was told it could not ignore. The dispute carried into the following fall.

leaders.name: Scott Whitehouse
leaders.note: ASG filed a formal reaction to the General Education Task Force proposal in 1988.
profile: Whitehouse won the March 1988 ASG presidential primary alongside Shannon Ragland, emerging from a field of seven candidates in a year when only two of 32 congress positions were contested.

He won the presidency on 7 April 1988, in an election the Herald's own editorial pages said had been marred by oversight and closed minds, and amid coverage of votes for a write-in candidate that the congress was told it could not ignore.

The disputed election shadowed his term into the fall: Bruce Cambron, who had demanded a new election in April, took his complaint to university president Thomas Meredith in October 1988, weeks after the congress banned future write-in campaigns. His year also produced ASG's formal written reaction to the General Education Task Force proposal.

events.title: A formal reaction to the General Education Task Force
events.body: ASG filed a written response to a proposed overhaul of general education requirements - one of the earliest surviving examples of student government intervening in curriculum rather than campus life.

events.title: Write-in campaigns banned
events.body: ASG approved a ban on future write-in campaigns, five months after write-in votes had thrown its own presidential election into dispute. An editorial the next issue said the block showed ASG was not listening.

events.title: Freshman election turnout called pretty good
events.body: Turnout in the ASG freshman election was reported as "pretty good." The same issue said the organization was working to make the importance of voting register with students.

events.title: Cambron takes his election complaint to the president
events.body: Bruce Cambron, who had called for a new election in April, talked to university president Thomas Meredith about the ASG election. The spring's disputed result was still alive six months on.

events.title: Half the open slots filled; shelters for shuttle stops
events.body: ASG filled half of its open congress seats and sought shelters and seats for campus shuttle stops. The following week the Herald editorialized that ASG's efforts directly helped and served students.

events.title: The weeklong Thanksgiving break is dropped
events.body: ASG dropped its push for a weeklong Thanksgiving break, three weeks after voting to seek one. In the same issue, members rated their own organization as average.

events.title: An extra study day recommended
events.body: ASG recommended adding an extra study day before exams. The proposal followed January efforts to find a way to print teacher evaluations.

events.title: More movie hours wanted
events.body: The congress asked for more movie hours on campus. It was one of the quality-of-life items that filled the spring agenda before election season.

events.title: Amos Gott edges Lynn Groemling
events.body: Amos Gott narrowly defeated Lynn Groemling in the ASG presidential race. The campaign season had drawn complaints from candidates about the brief primary and an editorial warning that name recognition should not decide the race.

leaders.name: Amos Gott
leaders.note: The best-documented pre-1992 presidency in the archive. Signed correspondence survives on extended library hours, the DUC flagpole, the stadium press box and a local pizza vendor dispute.
profile: Gott was a visible member before he was president, signing Herald letters on ASG's behalf, including a January 1989 piece promoting Campus Pride '89 and an earlier letter urging readers to understand the organization.
He won the presidency in April 1989, edging Lynn Groemling in a race that had drawn candidate complaints about the brief primary.

His presidency ran on correspondence: resolutions went out over his signature as memoranda to named administrators and answers came back. In spring 1990 he wrote to six administrators under Resolution 90-6-S seeking changes to the final exam schedule, part of a surviving file that also covers extended library hours, the Downing University Center flagpole, mace sales at the bookstore, AIDS education and larger diplomas.

events.title: Extended library hours
events.body: Correspondence between President Amos Gott, Howard Bailey, Sally Ann Strickler and Michael Binder. Resolutions went out as letters to named administrators and answers came back.

events.title: The Downing University Center flagpole
events.body: One item in a working inventory of the job that year: the flagpole, the stadium press box, a dispute involving a local pizza vendor and a proposed budget for the Board of Student Body Presidents.

events.title: Gott gets a jump on the semester
events.body: The Herald reported that Amos Gott had gotten a jump on the ASG semester, opening his presidency before classes settled in. A companion piece urged students to participate in the organization.

events.title: A budget tiny compared to other schools
events.body: The Herald reported that ASG's budget was tiny compared to student governments at other schools. Two days later the congress approved joining a new board but admitted it could not afford the membership.

events.title: Resolution 89-3-F asks for AIDS education
events.body: Under Resolution 89-3-F, ASG corresponded with administrators requesting education on AIDS, HIV and sexually transmitted diseases. The letters survive in the SGA records alongside the year's other resolution correspondence on mace sales, larger diplomas and a food services committee.

events.title: Student government goes to Glasgow
events.body: Student government went to the WKU Glasgow campus, and the congress agreed to look again at a Public Interest Research Group. Both stories ran in the same mid-October issue.

events.title: PIRG sunk over its fee system
events.body: ASG voted down the proposed Public Interest Research Group, saying its fee system was the culprit. The decision ended a semester of on-and-off consideration of the group.

events.title: Congress votes to expand
events.body: ASG voted to expand its congress, a week after reporting it might add representatives. A follow-up story said classes and student groups would get more voice in the organization.

events.title: Withdrawals save an invalid primary
events.body: Candidates withdrew from the ASG races, saving a primary that would otherwise have been invalid; only two candidates were running for president. The Herald had already reported that interest in the organization might be lower, illustrated by a cartoon of student government in an empty room.

leaders.name: Michael Colvin
leaders.note: Elected Associated Student Government president in results the Herald reported on 19 April 1990; the 1991 Talisman independently confirms him as Associated Student Government President for that year.

sources.label: Herald 65:55, 19 Apr 1990, "Michael Colvin Aces Associated Student Government Election"

profile: Michael Colvin won the Associated Student Government presidential election in results the Herald reported on 19 April 1990 under the headline "Michael Colvin Aces Associated Student Government Election." The 1991 Talisman independently lists him as Associated Student Government President for 1990-91.
In office, the Herald reported ASG considering a four-day class week (7 February 1991) and covered concern inside the organization over a change affecting student insurance (15 January 1991).
The archive does not preserve further detail of how the term ended or what Colvin did afterward.

Colvin took office in August 1990, introduced by the Herald as a new leader who wanted to make ideas reality. He had been active in the organization at least since September 1989, when he signed a Herald piece soliciting help for ASG.

His spring 1991 agenda was the widest of the era: in a single February week ASG moved to cap tuition boosts, proposed overhauling the Detrex registration system, and planned lobbying to protect student financial aid.
Letters he signed under Resolution 91-7-S survive in the SGA records, pressing administrators Kemble Johnson and Debby Cherwak for improvements to Detrex Field.

events.title: Michael Colvin elected Associated Student Government president
events.body: Colvin won the Associated Student Government's presidential election, the Herald reported under the headline "Michael Colvin Aces Associated Student Government Election."

events.title: ASG pushed for a higher student activity fee
events.body: The same Herald issue that reported Colvin's election win reported the Associated Student Government was seeking an increase to the student activity fee.

events.title: Regents set the 1990-91 tuition and operating budget
events.body: WKU's Board of Regents met in special session and approved the university's 1990-91 operating budget, tuition rates, and personnel changes ahead of Colvin's term.

events.title: Students held a campus vigil as the Gulf War approached
events.body: The same Herald issue covered a campus prayer vigil for peace as the U.N. deadline for Iraq's withdrawal from Kuwait neared, two days before the United States led a coalition into the Gulf War.

events.title: ASG looked at a four-day class week
events.body: The Associated Student Government considered the idea of moving to a four-day class week, the Herald reported.

src.label: Herald 66:39, 7 Feb 1991, "Associated Student Government Looks at Having Four-Day Class Week"
