leaders.name: Matthew Wininger
leaders.note: Sworn in as student regent 6 August 2021, at the meeting that renamed Northeast Hall for Margaret Munday, WKU's first African American student to enrol.
profile: Wininger ran for student body president in the April 2021 SGA election, with voting held on TopNet April 12-13. In the Herald's ballot guide he said he wanted to make SGA "the most active and vibrant organization on campus." Me'Lon Craighead, who would serve as his executive vice president, ran for that office in the same election.

As president, Wininger opened the fall semester by welcoming new and returning senators to the second meeting of the 21st Senate. He presided over the unanimous confirmation of senators elected the previous semester and of his executive appointments, including Jamison Moorehead as IT director, Alexis Courtenay as public relations director and Parker Raybourne as chief of staff, and the senate adopted new election codes at the same meeting.

In spring 2022 Wininger welcomed senators back from winter break and announced an initiative to create a student resource handbook aimed particularly at underclassmen, encouraging all SGA committees to pitch in on the project. At that same first meeting of 2022, the senate he led responded to the December tornado disaster by unanimously passing a $1,000 bill to restock the Office of Sustainability food pantry.

events.title: Northeast Hall renamed for Margaret Munday
events.body: Student Regent Matthew Wininger was sworn in at the Board of Regents meeting that renamed Northeast Hall for WKU's first African American student to enrol - the first building on campus named after an African American.

events.title: Cole Bornefeld elected with 49% of 1,448 votes
events.body: Alexis Courtenay took 40% and Olivia Feck 11%. Sam Kurtz and Garrison Reed were elected to the two vice presidencies.

events.title: SGA opened the fall term with confirmations and new election codes
events.body: SGA held its first meeting of the fall semester, the second meeting of the 21st Senate, with President Matthew Wininger welcoming new and returning senators. All senators present were confirmed by unanimous consent and sworn in by Chief Justice Holden Schroeder, along with executive appointments Jamison Moorehead as IT director, Alexis Courtenay as public relations director and Parker Raybourne as chief of staff. New election codes for the next semester also passed with unanimous consent.

events.title: Senate confirmed the year's budget
events.body: At the third meeting of the 21st Senate on Sept. 7, SGA passed Bill 1.21f, confirming its budget for the year. Dean of Students Martha Sales spoke on leadership, and Wininger announced a planned donor drive in partnership with at least four other student organizations. Chief of Staff Parker Raybourne announced a Hilltopper Hangout event for Sept. 24.

events.title: New senators seated and freshman election results announced
events.body: The senate unanimously voted in four new senate members, two judicial council members and Trib Singh as director of academic and student affairs. Speaker of the Senate Tess Welch introduced committees on legislative operations, student experience, mental health, sustainability, campus improvement, diversity and student outreach. That night the fall election results named Addison Falkner, Sam Kurtz and Jenna Wells freshman senators and Arivumani Srivastava the Gatton Academy senator.

events.title: 21st Senate passed its first resolution, on advisor evaluations
events.body: At its Oct. 5 meeting SGA passed Resolution 1.21f, addressing the lack of an advisor evaluation system, by a 21-2 vote, the first resolution of the 21st Senate. Bill 2.21f, barring the speaker of the senate from voting on legislation, passed 21-2, and two bills scrubbing outdated 2007-era bylaws passed by unanimous consent. Parking director Jennifer Tougas discussed a possible monthly parking tag subscription and campus bookstore operations.

events.title: Resolution condemning critical race theory bans passed 16-15
events.body: After weeks of debate, the senate passed Resolution 7.21f, which condemned the banning of critical race theory teachings in postsecondary education ahead of an anticipated bill in the Kentucky legislature. The vote was 16 in favor, 15 against, with two abstentions. Sponsor Olivia Blackmon said the measure was meant to ensure intellectual freedom in the curriculum.

events.title: EF-3 tornado struck Bowling Green, killing 11 in Warren County
events.body: An EF-3 tornado with 150 mph winds slammed into Bowling Green early on Dec. 11, killing 11 people according to the coroner and destroying homes and businesses across Warren County. Gov. Andy Beshear signed a state of emergency and President Biden signed an emergency declaration. The disaster shaped SGA relief efforts the following semester.

events.title: First 2022 meeting funded tornado-drained food pantry
events.body: At its first meeting of 2022, SGA passed Bill 1.22s by unanimous consent, providing $1,000 to restock the WKU Office of Sustainability food pantry, whose food and toiletries had been drained by the tornado recovery effort. Wininger announced an initiative to create a student resource handbook for underclassmen. Speaker Tess Welch announced spring election dates of April 18-19.

events.title: Syllabi clause, crosswalk resolutions and Title IX meetings passed
events.body: At its Feb. 15 meeting SGA unanimously passed Resolution 6-22-S to add an SGA-related clause to course syllabi, which the Herald reported would be the first of its kind in SGA history. Three resolutions supported new crosswalks below the Van Meter green space and on Chestnut and Normal streets, and Bill 6-22-S required a committee chair or delegate to meet with the Counseling Center director and Title IX coordinator each semester. The senate also approved a task force for the iWKU app and funding for a financial success workshop.

events.title: Judiciary Council cleared Bornefeld's campaign over student-all email
events.body: After several SGA members complained that presidential candidate Cole Bornefeld's student-wide email about the Swipe Out Hunger initiative violated the election code's ban on self-promotion, the Judiciary Council held a roughly hour-long Zoom hearing on April 13 and voted in favor of his campaign. Speaker Tess Welch argued the signed email constituted self-promotion, while a statement from President Wininger, read by Chief Justice Holden Schroeder, said nothing in the code required executive approval for a student-all email. Senators said the initiative saw a record number of donations after the email went out.

events.title: End-of-year allocations funded scholarships, organizational aid and planetarium donation
events.body: Hours before the 2022 election results were announced, the senate passed a slate of funding bills: $8,000 in organizational aid at $500 per applicant, and $15,500 across five scholarship programs including summer class, study abroad, ISEC book and Scholar Level scholarships, plus $500 to Black Student Alliance scholarships for the first time. The senate also approved $325 for the Hardin Planetarium, $500 for a student worker appreciation event, $300 for the CEC Run/Walk for Autism and $570.02 for an e-waste recycling bin on main campus.

leaders.name: Cole Bornefeld
leaders.note: Elected April 2022 with 49% of 1,448 votes. In February 2023 the Speaker of the Senate brought a censure case against him over anti-transgender posts he had liked on Instagram; the Judicial Council voted unanimously against censure, and a Title IX report seeking his removal was filed two days later. Last name currently on the plaque.
profile: Cole Bornefeld came to the presidency by an unusually fast route. He transferred to WKU from Volunteer State Community College as a junior, emailed then-President Matthew Wininger during his first week on campus, and was appointed a senator-at-large at their first meeting. He had not planned to run for president, but after senators urged him to, he formed a ticket the week of the filing deadline and won. He campaigned on programs he backed as a senator, including the Share-A-Swipe meal donation program and growing SGA's scholarship budget, which rose by $3,500 during his presidency. Adjusting to the office, he said it felt like "drinking out of a fire hose," and he sought advice from former student body presidents weekly.

Bornefeld opened the 2022-23 year with an executive retreat on Aug. 29 at the Cliff Todd Center, where his team set three priorities: a one-stop resource guide for students, a push to represent WKU's five regional campuses, which he said was "an area that I really don't think SGA has ever touched," and financial assistance for students as the year's underlying goal. He had met with the director of regional campuses the week before to start that work.

His spring semester was dominated by fallout from anti-LGBTQ Instagram posts he had liked. After the judicial council unanimously declined to censure him, the Queer Student Union removed SGA meetings from its list of campus safe spaces and said it would not associate with SGA until a public apology was released. Addressing the senate on Feb. 21, Bornefeld, who also served as student regent, said he "always commits to loving thy neighbor" but could not commit to always agreeing, tying his position to his Christian values and offering to meet any student over coffee or breakfast to discuss disagreements.

events.title: The Speaker takes the President to the Judicial Council
events.body: Speaker of the Senate Yulia 'Julie' Mishchuk requested a censure hearing against President Cole Bornefeld over anti-transgender posts he had liked on Instagram. Members of the Queer Student Union and both vice presidents attended. The Judicial Council voted unanimously against censure.

events.title: A Title IX report seeks the President's removal
events.body: Filed with Student Conduct. Under the constitution, removing an executive who will not resign requires written endorsement from at least 20% of the Senate, a wait of at least fourteen days and a two-thirds vote of the full Senate sitting as a court.

events.title: Sam Kurtz elected on an unopposed ticket
events.body: With Salvador Leon as administrative vice president and Annalise Finch as executive vice president.

events.title: Executive retreat set the year's goals
events.body: SGA's executive team held a formal retreat dinner on Aug. 29 at the Cliff Todd Center to set its agenda for the year. President Cole Bornefeld said the group was building a one-stop resource guide for students and trying to promote SGA at WKU's regional campuses in Elizabethtown, Fort Knox, Glasgow, Owensboro and Somerset. Speaker Julie Mishchuk said the underlying goal of the year was financial assistance for students.

events.title: First meeting filled senate and cabinet vacancies
events.body: At its first meeting of the year on Aug. 30, the senate approved all of President Bornefeld's nominees, including Juan Thomas, Will Hemenover and Sydney Denney as senators-at-large, Aniya Johnson as director of information technology, Donte' Reed as director of enrollment and student experience, and Isaac Kind and Garrett Baum to the judicial council. Administrative Vice President Sam Kurtz spoke on the budget and Chief Justice Holden Schroeder swore in the new members.

events.title: Fall election turnout doubled; Reed appointed to state council
events.body: Fall 2022 election results announced at midnight seated Rush Robinson, Callison Padgett and Rhett Helland as freshman senators, plus Neel Patel for Gatton Academy, Shy'Ante Williams as graduate senator and Salvador Leon Golib as international student senator. President Bornefeld said the vote total rose from 398 the previous fall to 805. SGA also announced that Vice President Garrison Reed had been appointed student representative on Kentucky's Council on Postsecondary Education, with a term running through June 30, 2023.

events.title: Senate approved five nominations and reviewed a shrinking budget
events.body: The senate unanimously confirmed five nominations, including Adan Canizalez as chair of student enrollment and experience and Miles Huff, a track athlete, to the judicial council. Administrative Vice President Sam Kurtz urged senators to sponsor more resolutions, which use university funds, because only about $39,460.76 remained of SGA's $100,000 annual budget for bills. Speaker Julie Mishchuk floated a constitutional amendment requiring every senator to sponsor at least one bill or resolution.

events.title: Voucher bills funded dental clinic, ID center and Preston Center
events.body: The senate unanimously passed Bill 28-23-S, putting $500 toward free teeth cleanings at the WKU Dental Health Clinic after voucher use rose 660 percent in the fall, and Bill 27-23-S, allocating $2,000 in discount vouchers split 60/30/10 among the Preston Center, the ID center and the dental hygiene clinic. A $260 bill funding a poetry mic night with the Talisman also passed with one nay vote. Former SGA President Matthew Wininger opened the meeting as guest speaker.

events.title: Narcan resolution aimed to put overdose spray in residence halls
events.body: SGA unanimously passed Resolution 2-23-S on Feb. 7 supporting placement of Narcan, an opioid overdose reversal spray, in WKU residence halls. SGA had planned to spend about $1,000 of its own budget, but a University of Kentucky harm reduction specialist helped secure the product through a government grant instead. Housing and Residence Life planned to install the spray in AED-style boxes across its 15 dorms by Aug. 1 to allow time for staff training.

events.title: Menstrual product legislation passed as QSU protested
events.body: At its Feb. 21 meeting SGA passed a resolution supporting menstrual product dispensers on the first floor of every academic building, a $200 bill to distribute 35 menstrual cups at tabling events, and $100 for a community relations survey. Queer Student Union president Alistar Flowers announced QSU had removed SGA meetings from its list of campus safe spaces after the judicial council declined to censure President Bornefeld, and said QSU would not associate with SGA until a public apology was released.

events.title: Election reform bill failed 19-15
events.body: Bill 39-23-S, which would have moved the transfer, non-traditional and first-generation senate seats to the fall election and required a two-thirds senate vote to convert vacant seats to at-large seats, failed 19-15, short of the two-thirds needed. Sponsor Neel Patel called the growing reliance on presidential appointments a dangerous practice for a government organization. The same meeting unanimously funded the April 3 Afro-Latinidad cultural event and rejected funding for Dance Big Red.

events.title: Senate merged committees and funded Mental Health Awareness Week
events.body: At the April 11 meeting the senate passed Bill 44-23-S, a constitutional amendment merging the Community Relations and Outreach committees starting in 2023-24, which Speaker Mishchuk said would create a stronger committee amid low membership. Senators also unanimously funded a slate of Mental Health Awareness Week events for April 23 through 28, including an Out of the Darkness suicide prevention walk, and passed a $62 terrarium tabling bill. President Bornefeld reported 44 applicants for the upcoming SGA elections.

events.title: WKU dedicated the Commons at Helm Library
events.body: WKU formally dedicated the $35 million Commons at Helm Library, a renovation funded through a partnership with Aramark, and President Timothy Caboni announced early plans for a similar makeover of Cherry Hall. SGA President Cole Bornefeld spoke at the ceremony, saying the building had been full of excitement and community since it opened.

leaders.name: Sam Kurtz
leaders.note: Former administrative vice president. Elected April 2023 on an unopposed ticket with Salvador Leon and Annalise Finch.
profile: Sam Kurtz, then the outgoing administrative vice president, was elected student body president in results announced early on April 19, 2023 in the Downing Student Union senate chambers, after voting opened on TopNet on April 17. His KFL ticket, with Annalise Finch as executive vice president and Salvador León as administrative vice president, ran unopposed, and Chief Justice Justin Goins read the results. In a statement, Kurtz said the ticket would "listen to students' concerns, represent their voices, lead with integrity, and promote transparency."

At the 23rd Senate's first fall meeting on Aug. 29, Kurtz nominated Ashley Ranger, Anna Kate Hardin, Ellen Henderson, Morgan Gammons and Garrison Reed to the Judicial Council from what he called a record number of applicants, and named seven committee heads, including Rush Robinson for Campus Improvements and Sustainability and Karley Solorzano for Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. The Senate's first bill of the year, passed unanimously that September, funded the SGA Pink Walk breast-cancer event. Speaker of the Senate Sydney Denney wrote or co-wrote several of the year's bills, including a resolution capping student parking fees at $50, a $700 fund to help students pay parking fines, and voucher funding for the Dental Hygiene Center and ID Center. In February 2024 Kurtz and Chief of Staff Donté Reed rolled out a 450-voucher Uber giveaway aimed at student safety and outreach.

The year's fight was internal. In February 2024 the Judicial Council voted 6-0 to censure Administrative Vice President Salvador León after a hearing brought by Denney and the executive cabinet, which alleged León had spent SGA funds - including a $425.25 Preston Center deposit for Neurodiversity Acceptance Week - before the Senate passed the funding bill, in violation of the constitution's clause 2.5.3 requiring the administrative vice president to expend funds only as the Senate authorizes. León countered that text messages showed Kurtz had signed off on the spending in advance; the council found the spending improper but recommended no discipline beyond the censure itself.

In January 2024 Chief of Staff Lindsey Kelly and enrollment director Donte Reed both resigned, with Reed moving up to chief of staff. That April, Kurtz ran for a second term with Reed as his executive vice president candidate and junior senator Ethan Taylor for administrative vice president; the ticket again ran unopposed, and the three were re-elected as the 24th Senate's 34 members were announced the night of April 16-17, 2024. The 23rd Senate held its last meeting on April 16 with no legislation on the agenda, and Kurtz thanked senators in his final report for what the group had accomplished that year.

events.title: The 23rd Senate corrects its own governing documents
events.body: Three bills from the Legislative Operations Committee: fix references to a 'University Senate' that had since split into separate Faculty and Staff senates, reconcile bylaws language about expelling senators with a constitution that only provides for impeachment, and update committee names that had drifted.

events.title: 23rd Senate seats Judicial Council and committee heads
events.body: At its first meeting of the fall semester, SGA approved President Sam Kurtz's nominations of Ashley Ranger, Anna Kate Hardin, Ellen Henderson, Morgan Gammons and Garrison Reed to the 2023-2024 Judicial Council after what Kurtz called a record number of applicants. Kurtz also announced seven committee heads, including Rush Robinson for Campus Improvements and Sustainability and Karley Solorzano for Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion. The new appointees took the oath of office at the meeting.

events.title: First bill of the year funds the Pink Walk
events.body: The 23rd Senate passed its first piece of legislation, Bill 1-23-F, at its fifth meeting. The bill allocated $500 from SGA's scholarship budget for the SGA Pink Walk, an October breast cancer awareness event for students and the Bowling Green community. It passed unanimously with 28 votes.

events.title: Fall election winners sworn in
events.body: SGA announced its fall election results on Sept. 20 over an Instagram livestream, electing Savanna Kurtz, Malick Ibrahim and Chloe Ralston as freshman senators, ShyAntye'e Williams as graduate senator, Sim Guan Zhou as international senator and Livi Ray as Gatton Academy senator. Five of the six were sworn in at the following Tuesday meeting. Sophomore senator Rush Robinson received the year's first Senator of the Month award.

events.title: Midyear resignations reshuffle the executive cabinet
events.body: President Sam Kurtz announced the resignations of Chief of Staff Lindsey Kelly and of Donte Reed as director of enrollment and student experience. The senate approved Kurtz's nominations of Reed as the new chief of staff and Sarah Vincent as director of enrollment and student activities. Kurtz also filled vacant transfer/non-traditional, sophomore and graduate senate seats with Sawyer Edmonds, Gabe Jerdon and Elizabeth Gannon.

events.title: Judicial council censures Salvador León
events.body: The SGA judicial council voted 6-0 to censure Administrative Vice President Salvador León after a Feb. 7 hearing on allegations that he spent funds, including a $425.25 Preston Center deposit for Neurodiversity Acceptance Week, before the senate passed the funding bill. León argued text messages showed President Sam Kurtz had accepted the spending, while Kurtz said he asked León multiple times not to spend before the bill passed. The council recommended no further disciplinary action beyond the censure.

events.title: Uber voucher program and parking fee measures
events.body: President Sam Kurtz and Chief of Staff Donte Reed announced a program of 450 Uber vouchers worth $10 each, distributed through social media giveaways, meeting attendance and SGA events. The senate also passed Resolution 18-23-S supporting a cap on student parking fees at $50 and Bill 19-23-S allocating $700 to help financially vulnerable students pay parking fines, along with $1,045 in Dental Hygiene Center and ID Center vouchers.

events.title: Funding for DEI Week and Spring Fling
events.body: At its 20th meeting the senate funded SGA Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Week, four days of themed tabling from March 25 to 28 covering mental health, campus demographics, sexual health and deaf awareness. A $450 bill for the SGA Spring Fling, whose proceeds went to the Kids Cancer Alliance, passed 28-2 after debate among senators over the amount being spent. A $280 bill funded a Hope Harbor Denim Day event for Sexual Assault Prevention Month.

events.title: 23rd Senate holds its final meeting
events.body: The 23rd Senate met for the last time with no legislation on the agenda, spending the meeting on senators' final remarks. Kurtz thanked the senate and said in his final report, "We've done a lot of great things this year." Executive Vice President Annie Finch and Administrative Vice President Salvador León also gave closing reports before the 24th Senate's first meeting on April 23.

events.title: Kurtz re-elected unopposed to a second term
events.body: Running with Chief of Staff Donté Reed for executive vice president and junior senator Ethan Taylor for administrative vice president, Kurtz was re-elected without opposition as the 24th Senate's 34 members were announced the same night. More than 60 students had appeared on the ballot for the spring 2024 general election.

senate.note: The 2023-2024 Judicial Council was Ashley Ranger, Anna Kate Hardin, Ellen Henderson, Morgan Gammons and Garrison Reed, nominated by Kurtz from a 'record number' of applicants (Herald, 30 Aug 2023). Justin Goins, chief justice of the outgoing Judicial Council, read the April 2023 election results; Isaac King was chief justice by the April 2024 town hall. Which of the two - or whether both - held the post across the 23rd Senate's term is not established.

leaders.name: Sam Kurtz
leaders.note: Re-elected unopposed. Warned the Senate repeatedly that an unusually senior chamber meant the 2025 election mattered more than usual.
profile: Kurtz opened the 2024-25 year presiding over the 24th Senate, which passed SGA's $100,000 budget at its first meeting on Aug. 27. Sitting down with the Herald editorial board alongside his executive cabinet, he described SGA as "a vessel for good" and a group of 45 to 50 people advocating for students, and credited President Caboni with keeping the budget untouched for several years.

Through the spring he presided over a run of student-welfare legislation, including the Gordon Wilson Hall elevator resolution and a resolution seeking 24/7 library hours during finals week. In February he announced a POLLapalooza push to raise election participation, telling the Senate, "My goal is that 3,000 students vote in our election."

Kurtz closed his term at the 24th Senate's final meeting on April 15, having served as student body president for two years and holding executive branch positions for most of his college career, and prepared to graduate at the end of the semester. He received a standing ovation after his last report, and his parting words to senators were "Please be for the students."

events.title: A mental health survey, and a warning about the election
events.body: The Senate passed Bill 4-25-S funding a DEI Committee tabling event to gather anonymous mental health survey responses. Dean of Students Martha Sales told the Senate 'you cannot isolate and educate at the same time'. Kurtz warned repeatedly that an unusually senior chamber made the spring election matter more than usual.

events.title: Rush Robinson elected on a turnout of 966
events.body: Elected alongside class, college, transfer, first-generation, Intercultural Student Engagement Center and Honors College senators - constituencies the 1966 constitution had no concept of.

events.title: Senate passed $100,000 budget at first meeting
events.body: At its first meeting of the year on Aug. 27, the SGA Senate passed a $100,000 budget for 2024-25, including $20,000 for organizational aid, $23,500 for scholarships and $10,705 in legislative discretionary funding. Executive leaders told the Herald editorial board they intended to spend the full allocation, and President Sam Kurtz credited WKU President Caboni with keeping the budget level for several years.

events.title: Fall election winners sworn in, school safety bill passed
events.body: Five senators elected in the fall election, three freshman senators plus an international and a Gatton Academy senator, were sworn in at the Oct. 1 meeting. The Senate passed three bills, including Bill 4-24-F to make school safety training mandatory for WKU professors and require posted emergency exits in classrooms, and two bills backing a Spooktober fundraiser for the Potter Children's Home Initiative.

events.title: Three senators removed for excessive absences
events.body: Senators Malick Ibrahim, Myricle Gholston and Karisha Petty were removed from their seats at a Nov. 6 censure meeting after each accumulated at least six unexcused absences from weekly senate meetings. The Judicial Council voted 7-0 to remove them under a constitutional provision requiring removal of any senator censured twice, calling the decision a matter of accountability rather than an attack on character.

events.title: Trump DEI order prompted constitutional review
events.body: Chief Justice Morgan Gammons said the SGA Constitution might require amendment to its diversity, equity and inclusion provisions after President Trump's executive order directing federal agencies to end DEI mandates. Gammons said the Judicial Council would meet to decide whether an amendment was needed, noting that WKU receives federal funding as a public university. The Senate also filled several appointed positions at the same meeting.

events.title: Resolution backed Gordon Wilson Hall elevator
events.body: The Senate passed Resolution 2-25-S supporting installation of elevators in Gordon Wilson Hall, prompted by wheelchair user Kiersten Washington, whose dance appreciation class was scheduled on the building's third floor. It also passed Resolution 1-25-S supporting 24/7 hours at The Commons at Helm Library during finals week, and Kurtz announced a POLLapalooza effort with a goal of 3,000 voters in the April election.

events.title: Resolution supported mental health advisory board
events.body: The Senate passed Resolution 4-25-S supporting the formation of a Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Advisory Board to advise upper-level administration on student mental health policy, with Dean of Students Martha Sales planned to oversee its creation. Co-author Emma Harris, the Resident Staff Association president, said Counseling Center staffing shortages had pushed students to rely on resident advisors. The Senate passed eight bills at the same meeting.

events.title: Senate voted to rename DEI Committee
events.body: Senators unanimously passed Bill 21-25-S, a constitutional amendment restructuring the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Committee and renaming it the Action and Opportunity Committee, following President Trump's executive order dismantling DEI mandates. The meeting initially lacked the 21 members needed for a two-thirds vote, so absent members were called onto Zoom to reach quorum. The amendment then went to a student referendum during the April 13-15 election.

events.title: Students ratified DEI amendment with 88% of vote
events.body: In the spring election, the student body approved Bill 21-25-S, the constitutional amendment renaming the DEI Committee to the Action and Opportunity Committee, with 88% of votes in favor. Committee chair Megan Farmer said the committee at its core was not changing and the rename was meant to better communicate its actions. Results for 31 senate seats were announced the same night.

events.title: 24th Senate held final meeting
events.body: The 24th Senate met for the last time on April 15 with no legislation on the agenda, spending the meeting on farewells. President Sam Kurtz, Vice President Donte Reed and Chief Financial Officer Ethan Taylor each received a standing ovation, and the Senate recorded 295 spring scholarship applications, far above the roughly 40-applicant average of past years.

leaders.name: Rush Robinson
leaders.note: Elected 13-15 April 2025 on a turnout of 966. Told the Faculty Senate to 'take a field trip' to see the state of WKU's residence halls. Handed his successor the red suit jacket on 28 April 2026.

profile: Robinson, a senior from Benton, Kentucky triple-majoring in psychology, philosophy and sociology and a member of Sigma Phi Epsilon and Omicron Delta Kappa, won the SGA presidency in the 13-15 April 2025 general election on a turnout of 966, running with Savanna Kurtz for vice president and Gabriel Jerdon for chief financial officer. He also succeeded Sam Kurtz as WKU's student regent; the Board of Regents administered his oath of office on 8 August 2025, the same meeting at which it named the new Gordon Ford College of Business building Amy and David Chandler Hall and elected Jan West chair, Doris Thomas vice chair and Melissa Dennison secretary for 2025-26.

Robinson ran on turning SGA away from national politics and toward direct student advocacy, saying the organization had sometimes echoed national political talking points and that he wanted it to act as "an advocate and resource for students" who could be pointed to the right contact in the administration. His cabinet - Kurtz as vice president, Jerdon as chief financial officer, Maggie Yelton as chief of staff, and Preston Jenkins, reappointed chief communications officer on 22 April 2025 and confirmed by the Senate - ran a legislative program heavy on small, direct-benefit measures: vouchers for CPR certification, dental cleanings, transcripts and identification cards, equipment to borrow such as umbrellas, calculators and hammocks, and a resolution urging accessible restroom stalls in Grise Hall. Jenkins also organized a student-painted mural for a column in the SGA chambers. In March 2026 SGA drew on its projects fund to host a baseball-game tailgate, a response to Athletics Director Todd Stewart's call for more student engagement.

At the Senate's first meeting under his successor, Robinson opened by telling the mostly-new chamber they looked untainted by SGA's usual troubles, then handed president-elect Caden Lucas the red suit jacket passed president to president - the same jacket Sam Kurtz had given him the year before. His term as student regent outlasted his SGA presidency: at the Board of Regents' 5 June 2026 meeting, his last as regent, he cast the lone vote against a $204, 1.69 percent tuition increase, saying the board had "to do whatever we can to not raise the tuition" to preserve affordability. Afterward he planned to remain at WKU for an Ed.S. in school psychology, aiming for a career as a school psychologist in a school district.

events.title: Robinson reappoints Jenkins chief communications officer
events.body: In one of his first acts after taking office, Robinson reappointed Preston Jenkins as chief communications officer; the Senate later confirmed the pick unanimously.

events.title: Robinson sworn in as student regent, succeeding Kurtz
events.body: The Board of Regents administered Robinson's oath of office as student regent, succeeding graduating president Sam Kurtz. At the same meeting the board elected Jan West chair, Doris Thomas vice chair and Melissa Dennison secretary for 2025-26.

events.title: Chandler Hall opened for the fall semester
events.body: The new Gordon Ford College of Business building, named Amy and David Chandler Hall after a $7.5 million gift and funded largely by a Kentucky General Assembly appropriation, opened to students on the first day of fall classes.

events.title: SGA commissioned a student-painted mural for the chambers
events.body: Chief Communications Officer Preston Jenkins announced a plan to have four student artists each paint one side of a column in the SGA chambers, incorporating WKU campus elements, with selections due by 19 September.

events.title: Senate revived the transcript voucher program
events.body: The senate passed Bill 24-25-F, authored by Legislative Operations Committee Chair Caden Lucas, allocating $195 to reestablish the transcript voucher program, giving students one free official transcript a semester. It also funded a new "Professor of the Month" award and ping pong equipment for the DSU recreation area.

events.title: WKU Restaurant Group answered senators' questions
events.body: Restaurant Group representatives fielded senator questions on the removal of Steak 'n Shake seasoning, kiosks in Subway and adding spicy chicken sandwiches to Chick-fil-A's meal-swipe menu, and said the service handled about 60,000 meal transactions a week.

events.title: CPR-voucher bill and Grise Hall accessibility resolution passed
events.body: The senate unanimously passed Bill 2-26-S, funding six vouchers for free CPR certification, and Resolution 7-25-F, supporting additional handicapped-accessible restroom stalls in Grise Hall after a student's father said the building had only one large stall.

events.title: SGA funded a tailgate to boost turnout at a baseball game
events.body: SGA used its projects fund to host free hot dogs, giveaways and a scholarship drawing before WKU baseball's home game against Louisville, an effort Robinson said answered Athletics Director Todd Stewart's call for more student engagement at games.

events.title: Weekly meeting funded a senior cookout, transfer cords and spikeball nets
events.body: SGA allocated $602.58 through three bills and a resolution: a senior sunset cookout, 240 transfer-student graduation cords, borrowable spikeball nets, and DSU signage improvements. CFO Gabriel Jerdon said the legislative discretionary fund would have $71.17 left if the following week's final bills all passed as written.

events.title: Robinson cast the lone dissenting vote on a tuition increase
events.body: At his last meeting as student regent, Robinson voted against a $204, 1.69 percent tuition increase that the rest of the Board of Regents approved, saying the board had to do everything it could to preserve affordability.

events.title: Two tickets take questions in the DSU auditorium
events.body: Caden Lucas with Jakob Barker and Will Derryberry against Jaden Marshall with Kaden Blankenship and Miles VanRude. Chief Justice Sophie Stirling moderated questions submitted by the student body.

events.title: Turnout jumps 66% in a contested race
events.body: 1,601 students voted, 635 more than the year before. Lucas won. The clearest evidence in the whole record that WKU turnout tracks whether there is an actual contest.

events.title: Robinson tells the Faculty Senate to look at the dorms
events.body: Sitting next to Faculty Regent Shane Spiller during a discussion of WKU housing, Robinson told senators to 'take a field trip' and see the state of the residence halls.

events.title: The red suit jacket changes hands
events.body: At the first meeting of the 26th Senate, Robinson handed Lucas the red suit jacket, "the one that Sam (Kurtz) gave me." The same night, Gabby Pace, Cayden Bailey, Maggie Phelps and Jaden Marshall were sworn in to their new roles.

leaders.note: From Harned. Beat Jaden Marshall in a contested race on a turnout of 1,601 - up 66% on the previous year. WKU Spiritmaster, chair of the Hilltoppers Vote Coalition, works for the City of Bowling Green's Downtown Development Division. Sworn in 28 April 2026 at the first meeting of the 26th Senate.

profile: Caden Lucas, a junior senator, WKU Spiritmaster, chairman of the Hilltoppers Vote Coalition and an employee of Bowling Green's Downtown Development Division, won the SGA presidential election on April 15, 2026, with running mates Jakob Barker for vice president and Will Derryberry for chief financial officer. Running under the motto "Lead, build, deliver," his campaign centered on increasing awareness of SGA operations and outreach to the student body, and he defeated Jaden Marshall, who had sought to become the first Black male student body president. After the results were announced Lucas said he felt "electric" and that the "work starts tomorrow," beginning with thank-you cards to supporters.

Lucas took office at the first meeting of the 26th Senate on April 28, 2026, where outgoing president Rush Robinson presented him with the traditional red suit jacket passed from president to president. Lucas thanked the new cabinet, nominated his defeated campaign opponent Jaden Marshall as an at-large senator, calling his campus work "phenomenal," and saw Gabi Pace and Cayden Bailey sworn in as chief of staff and chief communications officer. The meeting's speaker election deadlocked 9-9 between Amelia Tucker and Veronica Butler, a situation the governing documents did not address, and Butler won the seat in a re-vote.

Days after taking office, Lucas was named a 2026 Truman Scholar, WKU's second in the award's history and Kentucky's only recipient that year, chosen from 781 candidates nationally; the scholarship funds $30,000 toward graduate or professional study for students committed to public service. A political science, legal studies and strategic communications major, he had founded the Civic Engagement Resource Center as a Mahurin Honors College teaching fellow before taking SGA's top office. In May, WKU's Omicron Delta Kappa circle named him its Heather Strode Circle Leader of the Year, an award recognizing collaboration, inclusivity, integrity, scholarship and service.

Before he was sworn in as student regent, Lucas told the Herald he was "generally concerned" by a proposed $210 tuition increase; the Board of Regents approved a $204 increase days later, with outgoing regent Rush Robinson casting the only dissenting vote before handing the seat to Lucas.

events.title: Caden Lucas wins SGA presidential election
events.body: Caden Lucas and his ticket of Vice President-elect Jakob Barker and Chief Financial Officer-elect Will Derryberry won the spring election to serve during the 2026-27 academic year, defeating Jaden Marshall's ticket. Lucas, a junior senator, WKU Spiritmaster and chairman of the Hilltoppers Vote Coalition, ran on the motto "Lead, build, deliver" and a promise to make SGA operations more visible to students. The Herald did not publish vote totals or turnout figures; the story also listed the full slate of senators elected to the incoming 26th Senate.

events.title: 26th Senate seated; tie vote for speaker resolved in Butler's favor
events.body: At the first meeting of the 26th Senate, outgoing president Rush Robinson passed the traditional red suit jacket to Caden Lucas, and the body swore in Gabi Pace as chief of staff, Cayden Bailey as chief communications officer, Maggie Phelps to the judicial council and defeated presidential candidate Jaden Marshall as an at-large senator. The race for speaker of the senate ended in a 9-9 tie between Amelia Tucker and Veronica Butler, and Chief Justice Sophie Sterling confirmed that neither the constitution nor the bylaws addressed a tie. Outgoing speaker Hadley Whipple ordered a re-vote, which elected Butler as speaker.

events.title: Lucas voices concern over proposed tuition increase
events.body: WKU released a proposed 2026-27 budget that would raise tuition by $210 to $6,246 per semester within a $405.1 million operating plan. Lucas, identified as SGA president and soon-to-be student regent, said he was "generally concerned" by a proposal that would raise the cost of attending WKU. He said students deserved both a high-quality education and an affordable way to achieve it.

events.title: Regents approve tuition increase over student regent's lone no vote
events.body: The Board of Regents approved a $204 tuition increase to $6,240 per semester, the sixth consecutive yearly increase, along with a 5% housing rate increase and a 2% meal plan increase as part of a $405 million operating budget. Every regent voted in favor except outgoing SGA president Rush Robinson, casting his final vote as student regent before Lucas took the seat. The board also suspended several majors, including kinesiology and geological sciences, for reworking and mergers.

events.title: SGA got a new adviser in Student Activities leadership change
events.body: Andrew Rash, who had served as SGA's faculty adviser and Associate Director of Student Activities and Greek Life since 2022, became interim director of the Department of Student Activities on July 1 following the retirement of longtime director Charley Pride. Assistant Director of Student Activities and Leadership and Volunteerism Amelia Kolb took over as SGA's adviser going forward.

events.title: Executive candidates face off at SGA town hall
events.body: SGA held a town hall in the Downing Student Union Auditorium for the two executive tickets: Caden Lucas with Jakob Barker and Will Derryberry, and Jaden Marshall with Kaden Blankenship and Miles VanRude. Chief Justice Sophie Stirling moderated as the candidates answered 27 questions submitted by students. Both tickets made increasing awareness of SGA operations and outreach to the student body their central campaign promise.

events.title: Lucas named a 2026 Truman Scholar
events.body: Days after taking SGA's top office, President Caden Lucas was named a 2026 Truman Scholar, WKU's second in the scholarship's history and Kentucky's only recipient that year. The award, chosen from 781 candidates at 305 colleges nationally, provides $30,000 toward graduate or professional study and recognizes commitment to public service.

events.title: Lucas named ODK Circle Leader of the Year
events.body: WKU's Omicron Delta Kappa circle named President Caden Lucas its Heather Strode Circle Leader of the Year, an award for a student demonstrating leadership and dedication to the campus community across ODK's five core values.

officers.note: Won a re-vote after a 9-9 tie with Amelia Tucker; the governing documents had no tie-break procedure.

senate.note: Maggie Phelps was sworn to the Judicial Council and defeated presidential candidate Jaden Marshall was seated as an at-large senator, both at the 26th Senate's first meeting, 28 April 2026. The chief justice's name appears as both 'Sophie Sterling' (Herald, 28 Apr 2026) and 'Sophie Stirling' (Herald, 8 Apr 2026) in Herald reporting; unresolved which spelling is correct. No committee chairs had been reported as of this update - the 26th Senate's first fall meeting had not yet occurred.
